scenes.title: Complication and Resolution
scenes.summary: Every tragedy has a complication and a resolution, divided at the change of fortune, as in Theodectes' Lynceus.

scenes.title: Four Kinds of Tragedy
scenes.summary: The complex, the tragedy of suffering (the Ajaxes, the Ixions), the tragedy of character (Women of Phthia, the Peleus), and a fourth (the Daughters of Phorcys, the Prometheus, plays set in Hades).

scenes.title: Judging by the Plot
scenes.summary: Poets should try to excel in every part; tragedies are the same or different by their plots, and many tie the knot well and untie it badly.

scenes.title: Not an Epic Structure
scenes.summary: A tragedy must not try to hold a whole epic: those who staged the whole Sack of Troy or the whole Niobe failed, and so did Agathon.

scenes.title: Clever Villains Deceived
scenes.summary: Reversals aim at the tragic and the humane: the clever villain deceived, like Sisyphus; it is probable, as Agathon says, that the improbable should happen.

scenes.title: The Chorus
scenes.summary: The chorus should be one of the actors and share in the action, as in Sophocles, not as in Euripides; Agathon began the songs that could fit any play.
